PASSO 1: conte as posições. Um bloco, o: STEP 1: count the positions. One block, then the verb. Always in that order.
Em português, a ordem é flexível mas o s: In English, the subject sticks to the verb: "Today I live in Munich." Copy that into German and you get Heute ich wohne in München, which is wrong. In German, the verb never leaves second position. When anything other than the subject opens the sentence, the subject moves to after the verb: Heute wohne ich in München — literally "Today live I in Munich". English still does this in a few fixed phrases ("Here comes the bus", "Never have I seen…"); German does it all the time.
Quase todos os verbos alemães terminam e: Almost all German verbs end in -en in the infinitive. Drop the -en to find the stem and add the endings: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. Where English adds only one -s ("he works"), German changes for every person — but there are only five endings to learn. If the stem ends in -t or -d (arbeiten, finden), an extra -e- goes in before -st and -t, to make it pronounceable: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. If the stem ends in -s, -ß or -z (heißen, reisen), «du» loses the -s of its ending: du heißt, du reist. The «wir», «sie» and «Sie» forms are the same as the infinitive.
em português cada pessoa tem uma termina: English marks only one person in the present (he/she/it works). German marks almost all of them, but the pattern is short and regular, and «wir», «sie» and «Sie» simply repeat the infinitive. Good news: German has no "do" in questions or negatives and no -ing form — «Ich lerne» covers "I learn", "I'm learning" and "I do learn".
Raiz em -s: o «du» perde o -s da termina: Stem in -s: «du» loses the -s of the ending.

O verbo na segunda posição, perguntas e: Verb in second position, questions and negatives
O verbo conjugado fica sempre na 2ª posi: The conjugated verb always sits in 2nd position. If the sentence starts with something else (today, tomorrow), the subject moves to after the verb: «Heute arbeite ich.» In yes/no questions, the verb comes 1st — no "do" needed: «Wohnst du in Berlin?» (Do you live in Berlin?). In questions with a question word, the word comes 1st and the verb 2nd: «Wo wohnst du?» The negative «nicht» goes after the verb («Ich arbeite nicht» = I don't work) or before what it negates («Ich wohne nicht in Berlin»). To say you like doing something, put «gern» after the verb: «Ich lerne gern Deutsch» (I like learning German).
The conjugated verb goes in 2nd position.
Diga: «Heute arbeite ich. Wo wohnst du?: Say: «Heute arbeite ich. Wo wohnst du? Ich lerne gern Deutsch.»

PASSO 1: O erro que mais custa caro é de: STEP 1: the costliest mistake is keeping the subject glued to the front after a time or place word: Heute ich lerne. It feels natural because English does it ("Today I learn"), but in German the verb is a magnet fixed in position 2 and the subject moves after it (inversion). Two more English habits: adding a "do" (there is none: «Wohnst du hier?») and translating "I am learning" word for word (just «Ich lerne»).
